title: Chapter XLVI

teacherSummary.text: Letters from Jane report that Lydia has run off with Wickham, possibly not married. Darcy finds Elizabeth distraught; she confides in him. Elizabeth and the Gardiners hurry home.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XLVI,” how does Austen show scandal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XLVI, how does Austen develop the idea of scandal? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the plot in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLVI develops the idea of scandal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XLVI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its plot shape the reader's understanding of scandal. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XLVI suggests about scandal. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's plot and conflict), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XLVI to complicate the reader's understanding of scandal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of scandal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XLVI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of scandal follows or bends those conventions, using the plot as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XLVI and its treatment of scandal. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's plot and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XLVI as evidence for a larger claim about scandal in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of scandal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Elizabeth tell Darcy, and what does she fear? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: A 16-year-old runs away with an adult man. We will discuss who holds power here.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are fluctuating, actuated, superseded, informing, darting. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “Her affections had been continually fluctuating, but never without an object.” In this sentence it means: rising and falling; changing again and again. Word histories: “fluctuating”: From Latin fluctuare "to move in waves," from fluctus "a wave," from fluere "to flow." For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. An unmarried elopement could ruin the reputation of an entire family. Why does this chapter matter? The crisis tests Darcy's love and reveals Elizabeth's change of heart. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Without allowing herself time for consideration, and scarcely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth on finishing this letter instantly seized the other, and opening it with the utmost impatience, read as follows: it had been ” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to scandal? I circle “finishing”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find plot, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter XLVI develops the idea of scandal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about scandal, backed by one short quotation.

segments.script: Today we saw how plot shapes scandal. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
